paragraphs.heading: What the cycles are
paragraphs.text: Milankovitch cycles are the combined ways that slow changes in Earth's motion shape its climate over thousands of years. They take their name from Milutin Milanković, a Serbian geophysicist and astronomer. In the 1920s he worked out, in firmer numbers than James Croll had before him, how changes in the orbit's shape, the tilt of the axis and precession together alter where and when sunlight reaches the surface. He argued that this orbital forcing strongly steered Earth's climate patterns.

paragraphs.heading: Why Earth's motion changes
paragraphs.text: Earth's spin and its path around the Sun shift slowly over time, pulled by the gravity of other bodies in the Solar System. The changes are tangled, but a handful of cycles dominate. The shape of the orbit changes mainly because of the pull of Jupiter and Saturn. Because these motions alter how much sunlight arrives and where it lands, their effect is called solar forcing, which is one kind of radiative forcing.

paragraphs.heading: Three motions
paragraphs.text: The orbit stretches between almost a circle and a slightly oval shape, a property called eccentricity. A more stretched orbit means bigger swings through the year in Earth's distance from the Sun and in the sunlight it gets. The tilt of the axis, called obliquity, also shifts a little, and more tilt makes the seasons harsher. Then there is precession: the axis changes which stars it points toward, while the oval orbit itself turns. Together with eccentricity, precession means Earth's closest pass by the Sun falls in different seasons over time.

paragraphs.heading: The rhythm of the orbit
paragraphs.text: Eccentricity changes on several rhythms at once. Its largest swing repeats every 405,000 years, and other parts repeat every 95,000 and 124,000 years. These loosely blend into a cycle of about 100,000 years. Today the value is 0.0167 and falling, while the highest reached in the last 250 million years was 0.0679, and a perfect circle would score zero.

paragraphs.heading: Why 65 degrees north
paragraphs.text: Milankovitch paid special attention to latitude 65° north, because so much land lies there. Land changes its surface temperature faster than the sea, mainly because mixing between shallow and deeper water keeps the ocean surface fairly cool. The global ocean is also very slow to warm or cool, which delays changes in Earth's average surface temperature when other factors push it gradually.

paragraphs.heading: Seasons of unequal length
paragraphs.text: Right now Earth passes closest to the Sun, at perihelion, around 3 January, and is farthest, at aphelion, around 4 July. Earth moves fastest near perihelion and slowest near aphelion, so the seasons are not the same length. In the northern hemisphere this shortens winter and autumn: summer lasts 4.66 days longer than winter, and spring 2.9 days longer than autumn. Still, the orbit is so nearly round at present that the change in sunlight through the year matters less for the seasons than the tilt of the axis does.
